speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, the number of sexual misconduct cases across the autonomous universities (AUs) over the years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, the adequacy of law enforcement and disciplinary actions in deterring potential offenders.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Third, the support systems that have been put in place to help victims in a timely and effective manner that is sensitive to their needs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will address the first two aspects, while Second Minister Indranee will cover the final aspect.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, Members may want to pose your supplementary questions after both of us have given our replies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, incidence rates of sexual misconduct in the AUs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But there were another 14 cases committed by students that happened outside of campuses, making a total of 56 cases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I know that Mr Leon Perera, in his question, referred to cases within campuses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Twenty-five out of the 56 cases were from National University of Singapore (NUS); two from Yale-NUS which has its own Board of Discipline separate from NUS; 20 were from Nanyang Technological University (NTU); and six were from the Singapore Management University (SMU).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD), Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) and Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS) had one case each over the last three years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the number of cases for each AU is closely related to their student population.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As the student population changes from year to year, what is more meaningful is to express this as an incidence rate, that is, the number of sexual misconduct cases involving student perpetrators per 1,000 students.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The number was 0.21, 0.21 and 0.20 over the last three academic years, showing no discernible trend.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Of the 56 cases, the victims in 37 cases made Police reports.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Of these 37 cases, four cases are still under investigation and, for two, there was insufficient evidence to make out offences.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, there is a remainder of 31 cases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And these 10 are serious offences, involving outrage of modesty or multiple instances of voyeurism.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are all arising from Police reports and then Police action.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Minister Shanmugam will explain later how the Police deal with these cases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Separately, apart from Police action, the AUs will carry out their own disciplinary processes through their respective disciplinary bodies and mete out a combination of penalties that is within the AUs’ powers and authority.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These range from an official reprimand, which will be reflected in the student’s formal educational record, to suspensions, and expulsion, which is the harshest punishment an AU can administer.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To determine the appropriate sanctions, each case is evaluated by the disciplinary body, taking into account the severity of the misconduct and any mitigating factors, such as how remorseful and forthcoming the offender was during investigations, the potential for rehabilitation and the presence of any mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For offenders with psychiatric conditions, sanctions will include requiring the offender to start, or continue, with mandatory counselling and psychological treatment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Of the 56 cases I mentioned earlier that happened over the last three years, five cases are pending disciplinary hearings and four students withdrew from the university before sanctions were imposed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, out of the remaining 47 cases, 34 resulted in an official reprimand, 26 resulted in suspensions of up to two academic terms and 20 were banned from entering student dormitories.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These numbers do not add up to 47 because, typically, an offender received a combination of penalties.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if we just look at the 10 Police cases involving serious offences which led to jail sentences, there was only one expulsion, which was subsequently reduced to an 18-month suspension after appeal and the taking into account of the offender's psychiatric condition.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think there is no need for me to repeat my views on the adequacies of the penalties meted out by the AUs, but I will give two strong reasons why the AUs will need to review their disciplinary frameworks with a view to strengthening the penalties.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, we need to better balance the objectives of deterrence and redress for the victims against the rehabilitation of the offender.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Balancing these objectives is important for an education institution, but it should not end up with penalties that are too soft and too lenient.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our AUs are important national institutions that educate and nurture young Singaporeans to be contributing and responsible members of society.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To achieve this, the AUs' disciplinary frameworks should, therefore, be stringent but fair. "Two strikes and you're out" cannot be the standard application.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But neither should expulsions be the default for all forms of misconduct.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The penalty must continue to fit the offence, but there has to be a significant adjustment at the most egregious end of the spectrum of misconducts when they are serious criminal offences that undermine the safety and security of university campuses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We must ensure that potential offenders know the severe consequences of their actions, including the impact on their future.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And if the offender is remorseful, accepted and served punishment, he deserves a chance to make good.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is also the spirit behind the Yellow Ribbon project, and this is how we balance deterrence and rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second reason, we must recognise that voyeurism is a growing concern in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A recent "Big Read" article by TODAY published last weekend gave a good explanation that this may be because the young are exposed to the Internet from an early age, and technological advances make video-recording easier and more undetectable.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This led to some thinking that voyeurism is not a serious offence, and they cannot be more wrong.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Coincidentally, the Ministry of Home Affairs is amending the Penal Code, which will be debated this afternoon, to include new provisions on voyeurism.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the case of NUS, it has convened a Review Committee led by Mdm Kay Kuok, a member of its Board of Trustees, to review its disciplinary framework.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I know many students are not excited by Committees, but this is a necessary process to bring about a considered change to an established disciplinary framework.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Review Committee has started its work and will release its recommendations in stages.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the meantime, NUS management is taking immediate actions to improve the support systems and campus security, which Second Minister Indranee Rajah will elaborate on later.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ultimately, the AUs are tackling the concern on campus and student safety holistically, involving tougher penalties for offenders, better physical security on campus, and stronger support and greater sensitivity for the needs of victims.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This incident provided an opportunity for us to reflect on the character of our society.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I can see that we are a people with a strong sense of justice, who see the importance of differentiating between right from wrong, and this explains the strong reaction to Ms Monica Baey's situation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We also continue to believe in tough but fair systems of punishment to keep the Singapore living environment the way it has been.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These are characteristics of our society that I am proud of as a Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we should always refrain from trial by media, doxxing and resorting to mob justice.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: No matter how wrong an offender is, we need to respect the due process.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: During this episode, the harshest punishment for Nicholas Lim came from the social media.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I hope that, as a society, we will give his family and him the time and space they need to reflect on his actions, to turn over a new leaf and move forward.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They are strongly committed to doing so and I am confident there will be swift and meaningful changes, and my Ministry will work closely with them on these aspects.
